title: Rabbit
text: A hare is captured mid-leap, with its long ears pointing upwards and its body stretched out as if sprinting across the land. Its slender legs and sharp outline create a sense of speed and movement. Unlike many of the map’s more fantastic creatures, the hare resembles a familiar animal. Its presence reflects the Renaissance tradition of combining geographical information with illustrations of the natural world.

title: King of Portugal — Dom Sebastião
text:
The crowned king wears a richly decorated gold crown, a red robe, a blue collar, and an elaborate white ruff. He has a narrow moustache and a pointed goatee, presenting an image of royal authority and dignity. The banner beneath his portrait reads Il Re de Portogallo, meaning The King of Portugal.

The portrait is believed to represent Dom Sebastião, who ruled Portugal from 1557 until his disappearance and presumed death at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in Morocco in 1578. His disastrous military expedition left Portugal without a direct heir and triggered a succession crisis that led to the Portuguese Crown passing to Philip II of Spain in 1580.

The accompanying verse celebrates the king’s fame across the vast ocean and refers to fleets of armed ships travelling the seas. It reflects Portugal’s maritime prestige and the enduring reputation of its royal power during the Age of Exploration. Dom Sebastião’s disappearance also gave rise to Sebastianism, the legend that the lost king would one day return to save Portugal.

title: Philip II of Spain - The Royal Entourage
text: At the centre of this elaborate vessel sits Philip II of Spain, identifiable by his crown, red cloak and the inscription referring to “Re Philippo Max.” He is surrounded by two armoured figures, one raising an arm and the other holding a decorated shield. The throne-like vessel carries a royal banner and globe-like objects. Rather than depicting an ordinary voyage, the scene symbolises Spanish royal power and its far-reaching presence across the Atlantic and the Americas.

title: Goat — The Horned Wanderer
text: This mysterious goat-like animal has a shaggy body, slender legs and two enormous horns sweeping outward from its head. Its dark, finely drawn lines give it an almost mythical appearance. While the creature resembles a real goat or ram, the exaggerated horns make it look unusually imposing. Renaissance mapmakers often combined familiar animals with extraordinary creatures, reflecting a period when observation, inherited knowledge and imagination all contributed to how the world was pictured.

title: Bear — The Wild Beast
text: A stocky, bear-like creature stands on four short legs, its pale brown body framed by pointed ears and an open, red mouth. Its simplified form gives it a strangely animated expression, somewhere between a familiar wild animal and a creature from a medieval bestiary. The illustration is not detailed enough to establish its exact species with certainty. Its historical interest lies in the way early maps used animal imagery to represent the natural world beyond the familiar surroundings of European readers.

title: Cat — The Elusive Hunter
text: A slender feline moves across the map with its body held low, long tail extended behind it and narrow legs poised mid-stride. Its small head and alert posture suggest a wild predator. Although it may represent a leopard or another wild cat, the drawing lacks enough distinctive markings to confirm the species. In the sixteenth century, knowledge of exotic animals circulated through travel accounts, illustrated books and earlier maps. Such images brought distant wildlife into the European imagination, even when the animals were not depicted with scientific precision.

title: Cyclops — The One-Eyed Giant
text: This imposing human-like figure has muscular limbs, a rough garment and a large object carried over his shoulder. His face is presented as that of a Cyclops, the one-eyed giant of classical mythology. One of the most famous Cyclopes is Polyphemus, encountered by Odysseus in Homer’s Odyssey. The figure connects Monte’s map to the ancient stories that continued to shape European ideas about distant lands. In Renaissance cartography, classical mythology and geographical exploration could exist side by side, blurring the boundaries between the known world and the marvellous.

title: Dragon — The Armoured Reptile
text: This dragon-like creature has an elongated, scaled body, powerful jaws and a curled tail. Its most striking feature is the tall, fan-shaped structure rising from its back, divided into a series of geometric panels. The combination of reptilian anatomy and decorative armour makes it look like an animal from an imagined natural history. Dragons and sea monsters were recurring motifs in early maps, where they expressed the mysteries associated with distant regions and oceans. Researchers have also found that Monte adapted fantastic creatures from earlier cartographers, linking this image to a wider Renaissance visual tradition.

title: Crocodile — The Serpentine Predator
text: A long, green reptilian creature stretches across the map with a sinuous body, short limbs and a raised head. Its twisting shape gives the impression of an animal moving between land and water. Although interpreted here as a crocodile, its stylised appearance makes the exact species uncertain. Crocodiles were known through ancient natural-history writings and accounts of travel to distant parts of the world. In this illustration, the familiar idea of a dangerous reptile merges with the exaggerated forms commonly used for monsters in Renaissance maps.

title: Sea Snake — The Creature from the Deep
text: This strange marine creature has a broad, flattened head, mottled skin and a vivid red tongue. Two projections rise from its back, supporting a dramatic arch of fine, flowing strands that resembles a fountain or a mane. Its unusual anatomy makes it difficult to identify as an ordinary animal. Instead, it evokes the sea monsters that populated early modern maps, when sailors’ reports, classical literature and inherited legends helped shape ideas about ocean life. The image captures the sense that the sea remained a place of both discovery and uncertainty.

title: Urbano Monte — The Man Behind the Map
text: Inside a circular medallion, a bearded man looks outward with a composed, thoughtful expression. He wears a dark, patterned doublet and a large white ruff, the fashionable collar associated with elite European dress in the late sixteenth century. The surrounding inscription identifies him as Urbano Monte, the Milanese cartographer who created the map in 1587. His portrait is believed to show him at the age of 43. Monte assembled his vision of the world across 60 manuscript sheets, combining geographical information with history, natural imagery and imaginative creatures.

title: Two Dragons Fighting — Monsters in Conflict
text: Two fantastic reptilian creatures face one another with open jaws, as if caught in the middle of a confrontation. The creature on the left has a more elongated, winged form, while the one on the right has a heavily patterned back, raised spines and a tightly curled tail. Their contrasting bodies create a sense of movement and tension. Neither creature can be confidently linked to a particular named species or myth. Instead, they belong to the visual language of Renaissance cartography, where imagined monsters helped fill the world with stories, dangers and wonders.
